title: Pope Leo says liturgy reform calls faithful to active participation in worship
text:
Pope Leo says liturgy reform calls faithful to active participation in worship
LAX Leader
Pope Leo XIV said on Aug. 26 that the liturgical reform initiated by the Second Vatican Council was rooted in the Church's living tradition and aimed to encourage the faithful to celebrate the liturgy more consciously and actively, rather than as silent spectators.
Quoting Cardinal Giovanni Battista Montini of Milan, later Pope Paul VI, Pope Leo said, "The faithful 'cannot and must no longer remain silent and passive. Their physical presence cannot be reconciled with their spiritual absence.'" He delivered these remarks during his general audience talk in St. Peter's Basilica, focusing on "Sacrosanctum Concilium," the council's constitution on sacred liturgy.
This address marked Pope Leo’s final catechesis dedicated to the council’s first constitution after a series of talks begun Jan. 7 about Second Vatican Council documents. He previously said his intention was for people to reread and reflect on these texts directly instead of relying on hearsay or others’ interpretations.
Pope Leo said that while the reforms are firmly rooted in tradition, they must be properly understood: "A correct understanding of it also enables us to reject the abuses that occurred in certain sectors of the Church during the post-conciliar period, and which, unfortunately, still occur from time to time today, where some of the principles underlying the reform itself have been taken to extremes or misunderstood." He emphasized that participation by believers should not be passive because "the gestures and words of the sacred liturgy are critical" for experiencing a true relationship with God.
He added that language accessibility was important: there was a need "to make the richness of biblical texts and prayers more accessible" and streamline celebrations compared with previous practices. The pope described liturgy as “a living entity” subject to development over centuries; thus he said it is not surprising that revising liturgical books became necessary after careful respect for tradition.
In conclusion, Pope Leo quoted from Sacrosanctum Concilium: “the liturgy is made up of immutable elements divinely instituted, and of elements subject to change,” which may or ought to be changed if out of harmony with its nature. In his summary for English speakers, he said such changes help Christians “recognize sacred realities” and become more open to receiving God's grace.
